study.title: Ruth 2 - Providence, generosity and protection in the field of Boaz
study.overview: Ruth 2 shows how God's faithfulness acts in the midst of poverty and vulnerability. Ruth, a foreign widow, goes out to gather ears and, unknowingly, arrives in the field of Boaz, a relative of Elimelech. The chapter highlights Boaz's goodness, the dignity of Ruth's work, God's care for those in need and the hope that begins to be born to Naomi and his daughter-in-law. The text advances from the seemingly casual encounter to a concrete protection and the abundant provision that points to the action of divine providence.

outline.title: Ruth arrives at the camp of Boaz
outline.explanation: The chapter begins by introducing Boaz as Elimelech's relative and showing Ruth asking for permission to collect ears. She goes to the field and, without planning, enters the ground of Boaz, which the text presents as a providential event.

outline.title: Boaz welcomes and protects Ruth
outline.explanation: Boaz greets the workers, asks about Ruth, listened to her account and shows special care to her. It encourages you to stay in your field, guarantees protection against abuses, offers water and food, and guides your workers to facilitate harvesting from it beyond the minimum required.

outline.title: Ruth back with abundance and hope
outline.explanation: Ruth works until the end of the day, returns with a lot of barley and shares with Naomi what he received. Naomi recognizes in Boaz the goodness of the Lord and remembers that he is one of the family's redeemers. Ruth continues to reap with the girls of Boaz until the end of the harvest, while remaining with her mother-in-law.

study.context: The chapter presupposes the custom of allowing the poor to collect what was left of the harvest, a practice mentioned in the notes as a means of provision for the needy. It also presupposes the family structure of rescue, in which a relative could act in favor of a widow and preserve the lineage and inheritance of the family. The scenario is Belém and its fields, but the focus of the chapter is not in geographical details, but in the daily life of the harvest and in the care relations between relatives, workers and foreigners.
study.theology: Ruth 2 reveals God's providence discreetly but real: a simple decision to go into the field ends leading Ruth to the place prepared by God. Boaz's goodness is not only social courtesy; it expresses God's mercy toward the poor and vulnerable. The chapter also values the dignity of work, the protection of the weak and the generosity that goes beyond the legal minimum. At the same time, Naomi's faith begins to reappear when she realizes that the benevolence received is not mere chance, but an expression of the Lord's faithfulness. In evangelical reading, this movement prepares the redemptive hope that goes through the book, without the text having to declare everything immediately.

scholarViews.insight: The field of Boaz is presented as a fruit of divine providence, for the reapers should leave grain for the poor, and so God provided food to the needy.
The narrative highlights the humility and diligence of Ruth, as well as the fact that the providence led her to the field of Boaz.
Boaz orders Ruth to reap even among the beams, which gives him a greater privilege than the common custom of the repiga.

questions: How does God's providence appear in simple and common choice, like the work of a day in the field?
What does Boaz's behavior teach about generosity that protects the dignity of the needy, and not just gives him the least?
In which areas of Christian life do we need to imitate Ruth's diligence and the practical goodness of Boaz?
study.practice: Look for a concrete way this week to exercise generosity that goes beyond the minimum: to help someone vulnerable with respect, without humiliating, and without waiting for return. It is also worth observing how God may be conducting small and common steps of his routine for greater purposes. As Ruth, be diligent; as Boaz, be welcoming; like Naomi, learn to recognize the goodness of the Lord in the midst of need.
study.uncertainty: The available notes are limited and do not clarify all the historical details of the repiga system or the legal role of the remator; therefore, contextual reading was maintained only in what is supported by the notes and the chapter itself. Matthew Henry's comment was summarized from the excerpt provided, which was also incomplete in some excerpts.
